summary: Barnard's Star is a small, cool red dwarf about 6.0 light-years away, the fastest-moving star across our sky. Comparing images from 2010 and 2026, WANDERERS saw it shift 163 arcseconds, a speed of 10.40 arcseconds per year, matching Gaia DR3's 10.39 to within 0.1%, so we are highly confident. It is too bright for SPHEREx: all 188 measurements are flagged as overloaded, so there is no reliable spectrum. Its brightness change, +0.03 ± 0.03 magnitudes, measured from the star's outer glow, is too small to call real.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Three checks agree. From 2010 to 2026 it moved 163 arcseconds, about 26.6 SPHEREx pixels. Its measured speed of 10.40 arcseconds per year matches the Gaia DR3 value of 10.39 to within 0.1%. Gaia also lists this star directly, at 6.0 light-years away. One caveat: the star is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 188 measurements are flagged. Its brightness change (+0.03 ± 0.03 mag) could only be estimated from the star's outer glow.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: The motion is solid: 10.40 arcseconds per year measured against 10.39 from Gaia DR3. A big gap between those would make me doubt it. The brightness is the weak spot. All 188 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because the star is too bright for the detector. The +0.03 magnitude change was measured from the star's outer glow, and it is no larger than its ±0.03 uncertainty, so it may not be real.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this sky in 2010 and SPHEREx in 2025 and 2026. Over that 16-year gap, Barnard's Star moved 163 arcseconds, about 26.6 SPHEREx pixels. That works out to 10.40 arcseconds per year, which matches Gaia's 10.39. SPHEREx's own visits are only months apart. One caveat: the star is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 188 of its measurements are flagged and we show no spectrum.
